La lutte anti-raciste et décoloniale est: The anti-racist and decolonial struggle is on everyone’s lips. Since the death of George Floyd, that of Joyce Echaquan and the discovery of mass graves at Indigenous residential schools, governments can no longer ignore these issues. As Canadians head to the polls on September 20, systemic racism and reconciliation are emerging as an election issue.
Au-delà des intentions, quelles mesures: Beyond good intentions, what measures are elected officials proposing to fight these problems, which affect so many Canadians?
Pour lutter contre le racisme systémique: To fight systemic racism, the Liberals want to increase funding for Canada’s Anti-Racism Strategy, which the outgoing government put in place in 2019 with an investment of $45 million. If re-elected, the Liberal Party proposes to invest another $93 million in it between 2022 and 2026. “We will build on the progress made over the past six years and increase investments in community-led anti-racism education initiatives and programs that are essential to fighting hate and racism in local communities,” the party says. The Liberal Party also proposes an investment of $50 million over five years to support media led by racialized people, $200 million for Black-led organizations and $30 million to support Black researchers.
‍<strong>Le NPD</strong> souhaite mettre: ‍The NDP wants to push for the collection of race-based data to improve the lives of racialized communities, particularly in health, employment and police intervention. The party wants to look into employment discrimination based on ethnic origin and to close the resulting pay gap through legislation. It also talks about ensuring equitable, diverse hiring in the public service. The Green Party is the only federal party that wants to implement the recommendations of the report of the United Nations Working Group of Experts on People of African Descent on its mission to Canada. It has stated its intention to eradicate systemic discrimination in the federal public service and public institutions, in law enforcement, and in services for immigrants and refugees.
Sans faire jamais mention de racisme sys: Without ever mentioning systemic racism, the Bloc Québécois wants to use anonymous résumés in its public service to fight discrimination in hiring.
Rien dans la plateforme électorale <stro: Nothing in the Conservatives’ election platform mentions racism.
La GRC est dans la mire des partis alors: The RCMP is in the parties’ sights, as the Liberals, the New Democrats and the Greens cite the discrimination that Black and Indigenous people disproportionately suffer at the hands of the police service. The outgoing government wants to begin a reform that would re-examine the use of force, officer training, the involvement of social and community workers, disciplinary sanctions and the handling of complaints. For its part, the NDP pledges to put an end to police violence and carding.
Ils souhaitent revoir le budget alloué à: They want to review the RCMP’s budget, its training and its use-of-force techniques, with investments redirected toward non-police interventions, such as mental health and addiction support services. The party wants to tackle the overrepresentation of Black and Indigenous people in the prison system. They promise to work hand in hand with Indigenous communities to review the criminal justice system and to put in place an Afro-Canadian Justice Strategy.
Des réformes seront également mises en p: Reforms will also be introduced to end systemic discrimination against Indigenous people in the justice system, with legislative changes and funding for community-based healing justice and restorative justice programs.
‍<strong>Les verts </strong>veulent revo: ‍The Greens want to review and limit the RCMP’s role as well as its funding. The party urges divesting from services for which police are not suited, and wants to end street checks, identity checks, and arbitrary arrests and detentions. The party calls for decolonization, decriminalization and decarceration by strengthening laws in this regard. They are calling for criminal justice reform and a review of the prison system, where Indigenous and Black citizens are overrepresented, in order to develop a restorative justice model. These issues are not mentioned in the election platforms of the Conservatives and the Bloc Québécois.
Concernant la lutte contre la haine, <st: When it comes to fighting hate, the Bloc Québécois and the Conservative Party have no plan. The Greens’ platform, which is not costed, includes a plan to fight identity-based hate. They want to condemn extremist ideologies that encourage violence, fund the collection of data on the spread of hate, and support research and advocacy groups working to fight online hate and offline incidents. For its part, the NDP also proposes a pan-Canadian action plan to dismantle far-right organizations and to set up a task force to fight online hate. The party wants to establish standards for recording hate crimes and their treatment in the courts. It also proposes creating a task force to fight online hate, as well as more mental health resources for victims of hate crimes. “The CRTC’s powers could also be strengthened to actively fight this harmful phenomenon,” the New Democrats told us by email.
Seul le <strong>parti Libéral</strong> s: Only the Liberal Party is putting forward the National Action Plan on Combatting Hate, which would be put in place by 2022. The party says the plan will include recommendations from the Summit on Islamophobia and the Summit on Antisemitism. At the Summit on Islamophobia, one recommendation called for creating a fund for people who lost their jobs because of Bill 21. Asked about this at a press conference, Justin Trudeau did not say whether he would implement that recommendation. The Liberal platform also includes measures to fight hate-motivated crimes in Canada, and mentions possible amendments to the Criminal Code, training for public safety agencies and prevention of radicalization leading to violence. $10 million would also be invested in a National Support Fund for Survivors of Hate-Motivated Crimes. “I think all the platforms have shortcomings,” says Sanaa Ali-Mohammed, who took part in the Summit on Islamophobia held last July. She particularly laments that the problem has been relegated to the level of interpersonal discrimination rather than structural discrimination.
« Elle est omniprésente dans la plupart: “It is pervasive in most of the institutions of Canadian society,” says the researcher from the Diversity Institute. “One of the ways we see Islamophobia manifest itself really effectively is actually in employment and education, where it has a significant impact on people’s ability to earn an income and to access socio-economic progress and well-being, but that is not explicitly recognized anywhere,” Ms. Ali-Mohammed points out.
<strong>Les libéraux, le NPD et les vert: The Liberals, the NDP and the Greens have justice strategies for racialized communities. These parties, along with the Bloc Québécois and the Conservatives, all include a section on reconciliation with Indigenous peoples.
Sipi Flamand, vice-chef des Atikamekw de: Sipi Flamand, vice-chief of the Atikamekw of Manawan. Even so, the filmmaker wants to see more than awareness. “The federal government has recognized systemic racism, but I believe they need to go much further, so that the recognition is not just for show and concrete actions are actually taken,” he adds. In the 2015 federal election, the Liberal Party of Canada addressed reconciliation with Indigenous peoples. “It was another hopeful moment for Indigenous communities. In my analysis, the Liberal Party did not meet its objectives,” says Mr. Flamand, six years later. He particularly denounces the delays in addressing drinking water, with 50 advisories still waiting to be lifted in Quebec communities. All parties said they want to continue their efforts to restore access to drinking water as quickly as possible.
<strong>Principe de Joyce: la sonnette d: Joyce’s Principle: sounding the alarm on health and rights Sipi Flamand points to the efforts under way with the bill on Indigenous health, as well as the discussions on Joyce’s Principle, a brief submitted by the Atikamekw Council of Manawan and the Atikamekw Nation Council that defends Indigenous rights in Quebec and Canada in health and social services. The principle requires that all Indigenous peoples have an equal right to the best possible physical and mental health care, including a right of access to traditional medicines.
Le <strong>parti</strong> Vert ne mentio: The Green Party does not mention Joyce’s Principle in its platform. “The Green Party is in favour of applying Joyce’s Principle and the right of peoples to self-determination,” the party’s French-language spokesperson, Clément Badra, told us. The Conservatives do not address Joyce’s Principle in their platform and did not respond to our questions on the subject.
Le vice-chef atikamekw souhaite que les: The Atikamekw vice-chief wants change to happen just as much outside health care. In his view, a good starting point is Bill C-15, tabled by the outgoing Liberal government, which aims to harmonize Canadian laws with the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). “I think that with this law, we can begin to bring about changes in policy and administrative relationships,” Mr. Flamand explains. The Liberal Party, the Green Party and the NDP pledge to implement UNDRIP by working jointly with Indigenous communities. The Bloc Québécois will ensure it is implemented within its jurisdictions, and the Conservatives only talk about respecting Indigenous rights to the economic benefits arising from the exploitation of their territories, as set out in UNDRIP. The next step, according to the vice-chief? Files concerning territories and recognition of ancestral rights, an issue that affects all Indigenous peoples.
« Il faut que le gouvernement du Canada: “The Government of Canada needs to create a commission on treaties and on comprehensive and specific negotiations with Indigenous peoples,” he says. For now, only the Green Party has expressed a willingness to honour treaties and land claims and to create a law to that effect. Mr. Flamand also hopes the election promises can be fulfilled, and that the government in power, once elected, shows a willingness to reach understanding and to build relationships with Indigenous communities. “Indigenous peoples mobilized to go to the polls, notably many young people. That means Indigenous people are interested in politics, but that they want their fair share in Canadian politics.”
Le <strong>Nouveau Parti démocratique</s: The New Democratic Party plans funding to search for burial sites at former residential schools. Its budget proposes $10 million to be allocated to the Aboriginal Healing Foundation, but mentions no specific fund dedicated to searching for burial sites. Its platform also mentions appointing a special prosecutor to pursue those responsible for the harms, and covering the costs of community-based healing solutions.
Le <strong>Bloc québécois</strong> veut: The Bloc Québécois wants to put in place the measures needed to access church archives, and to ensure funding for programs to help victims heal, notably the Health Support Program.
Le <strong>Parti libéral</strong> présen: The Liberal Party platform includes an investment of $598 million to establish a strategy focused on First Nations mental health and well-being. An additional $83 million would go toward locating burial sites, allowing communities of origin to bury their own and hold the necessary ceremonies. The party proposes creating the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation and pledges $100 million for community initiatives aimed at transforming former residential schools into memorial sites. In honour of survivors, the Liberals propose building a national monument in Ottawa.
Le <strong>Parti conservateur</strong> s: The Conservative Party also wants to build a national monument in Ottawa. Its platform also proposes developing a plan that would allow for implementation of Calls to Action 71 to 76 of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, in the Missing Children and Burial Information section. Those calls include funding the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation, informing affected families of the location of their children, and developing strategies to maintain Indigenous cemeteries. The Conservatives talk about funding an inquiry into Canada’s Indigenous residential schools and deploying resources and honouring the people discovered during the inquiry.
Le<strong> Parti vert</strong> parle de: The Green Party talks about funding Indigenous healing centres to address the trauma caused by residential schools, as well as recognition and apologies, without mentioning excavations.

Le <strong>Parti conservateur</strong> p: The Conservative Party plans to develop, in collaboration with Indigenous groups, a National Action Plan to address violence against Indigenous women and girls.
